ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
On April 23, 2021, a new generation of high-speed maglev train developed in China was showcased at the first Chengdu International Industrial Expo, with a speed of up to 600 kilometers per hour, bridging the gap between aviation and high-speed rail. In a braking performance test, the train first started from rest on a straight track with rated power $P$, reaching its maximum speed $v$ after time $t$, and then entered a circular turning track in the horizontal plane at a constant speed. The mass of the train is $m$, the resistance during motion is constant, and the gravitational acceleration is $g$.

1. Find the distance $x$ traveled by the train as it accelerates from rest to its maximum speed $v$.
2. To allow the train to pass through the curved track at speed $v$ without lateral compression, the track is tilted inward at an angle $\theta$. Determine the design radius $r$ of the circular track.

Reasoning: The train starts from rest and accelerates with rated power P for time t until it reaches maximum speed v. The resistance force is constant. At maximum speed, the acceleration is zero, so the traction force balances the resistance. Since power at speed v is P = Fv, the resistance is f = P/v. During the acceleration interval, the engine input work is Pt, and the resistance does negative work fx over distance x. By the work-energy theorem, Pt - fx = (1/2)mv^2. At maximum speed, acceleration is zero, so the resistance force equals the traction force at speed v: f = P/v. Apply work-energy over the acceleration distance x: input work Pt minus resistance work fx equals final kinetic energy 1/2 mv^2. Substitute f = P/v and solve for x to get x = vt - mv^3/(2P). Resolve N vertically and horizontally: N cos theta = mg and N sin theta = mv^2/r. Divide to obtain tan theta = v^2/(rg), hence r = v^2/(g tan theta).

Model the acceleration phase dynamically. Let speed be u. The driving force at any nonzero speed is P/u because power P = F_drive u. Since v is the maximum speed, the constant resistance is f = P/v. The equation of motion is m du/dt = P/u - P/v. Instead of explicitly solving u(t), multiply by u and integrate over time from 0 to t: m u du/dt = P - (P/v)u.
